cases.title: Thirty thousand open files, folded twice
cases.why: `lsof` repeats a process's rows one per open file. The compactor collapses each run, and when the collapsed view is still too long a second pass folds THAT — so the answer has to say what the lines it dropped stood for.
cases.note: The listing is generated by reports/showcase/fx/lsof_shaped.py, not captured: a real `lsof` carries usernames, home paths and socket peers, and this corpus is published. The shape is what is being measured — long runs per process, and enough distinct runs that the collapsed view is folded again. Measured with the compactor alone (`tokenade filter`), which is reproducible — it cannot be answered by the exec-dedup layer. Above ~5000 tokens `tokenade wrap` additionally PARKS this result and hands back a short summary plus a recovery hash, so through `wrap` an agent receives far less than the figure here. The number below is what the compactor produces, not what `wrap` delivers.

cases.title: Which files have an unusual ACL, out of a whole tree
cases.why: A recursive ACL listing is one seven-line record per file, and on a normal tree they are all the same record. The reason to run it is to find the paths where they are not. The fold groups the tree by the ACL itself — every distinct one shown once, rarest first, with its count and a few example paths — so the three files that differ are named while the other 400-odd collapse into one block. cases.note: Measured on a synthetic tree (reports/showcase/fx/getfacl_tree.txt): the owners, groups and paths are invented. Its shape is what the fold is about — two common ACLs over ~440 paths, plus three files that differ.
